content: Cefiderocol is indicated for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI), including pyelonephritis, caused by susceptible Gram-negative microorganisms. The recommended dosage is 2 grams administered intravenously every 8 hours for a duration of 7 to 14 days. The length of therapy should be determined based on the severity of the infection and the patient’s clinical status, with a maximum duration of 14 days. Cefiderocol is also indicated for the treatment of hospital-acquired bacterial pneumonia and ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia (HABP/VABP) caused by susceptible Gram-negative microorganisms. The dosage and duration of treatment are the same as for cUTI: 2 grams intravenously every 8 hours for 7 to 14 days. To minimize the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain the effectiveness of antibacterial drugs, cefiderocol should only be used to treat or prevent infections that are proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. When culture and susceptibility data are available, they should guide the selection or modification of antibacterial therapy. In the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns may inform empiric therapy. The safety and efficacy of cefiderocol have not been established in certain populations. Elderly patients are more likely to have reduced renal function, so dose selection should be cautious, and renal function should be monitored closely. Cefiderocol may decrease the effects of oral microbiota-based therapies due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antibacterial agents, including cefiderocol, may reduce the efficacy of microbiota-based therapies if co-administered. It is recommended to complete antibiotic regimens 2 to 4 days before initiating microbiota-based therapies. Cefiderocol increases the toxicity of aminoglycosides such as amikacin, gentamicin, kanamycin, neomycin, plazomicin, streptomycin, and tobramycin through nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Caution and close monitoring are advised when co-administering these drugs. Cephalosporins, including cefiderocol, may enhance the nephrotoxic effects of aminoglycosides. Cefiderocol may decrease the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors, including atezolizumab, avelumab, balstilimab, camrelizumab, cemiplimab, cosibelimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, retifanlimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab, through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are recommended during co-administration, as this interaction may interfere with the therapeutic efficacy of these agents. Cefiderocol may increase the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Close monitoring is advised when these drugs are co-administered. Severe hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis and serious skin reactions, have been reported with cefiderocol. These reactions are more likely in individuals with a history of beta-lactam hypersensitivity or sensitivity to multiple allergens. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if an allergic reaction occurs. Cephalosporins, including cefiderocol, may trigger seizures and other central nervous system (CNS) adverse effects such as nonconvulsive status epilepticus, encephalopathy, coma, asterixis, neuromuscular excitability, and myoclonia. These effects are more likely in patients with a history of epilepsy or when recommended dosages are exceeded due to renal impairment. If CNS adverse reactions, including seizures, occur, a neurological evaluation should be performed to determine whether to discontinue treatment. Dosage adjustments are required for patients receiving continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), including CVVH, CVVHD, and CVVHDF. The dosage should be based on the effluent flow rate, and changes in residual renal function during CRRT may necessitate dosage modifications. Prescribing cefiderocol in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication is unlikely to provide benefit and may increase the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. There are no available data on the use of cefiderocol in pregnant women to evaluate the risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Data from published studies on cephalosporin use in pregnant women have not established drug-associated risks for these outcomes. It is unknown whether cefiderocol is excreted in human milk, but cefiderocol-derived radioactivity has been detected in the milk of lactating rats. When a drug is present in animal milk, it is likely to be present in human milk. No information is available on the effects of cefiderocol on the breastfed infant or milk production. Cefiderocol infusions should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration prior to administration. The solution should be clear and colorless. Any unused solution in the vial should be discarded. Unused vials should be refrigerated at 2–8°C (36–46°F), protected from light, and stored in their carton until use. Reconstituted vials can be stored for up to 1 hour at room temperature, and any unused reconstituted solution should be discarded.
